role.en: German ethnographer, geographer, and collector; disciple of Adolf Bastian
role.fil: Alemang etnograpo, heograpo, at kolektor; alagad ni Adolf Bastian
role.de: Deutscher Ethnograf, Geograf und Sammler; Schüler Adolf Bastians

portrait.alt: Tinted studio portrait of Wilhelm Joest, a man with a long forked beard in a dark jacket and patterned tie

quote.en: Doctor Wilhelm Joest has written to me and asked whether the box you have there can be opened. I have nothing to say against it; certainly, I sent the box to the museum, and if I sent it to Doctor Jagor and not to you, it is because Doctor Jagor was the one who first told me about it. I apologize for that.
quote.fil: Sumulat sa akin si Doktor Wilhelm Joest at itinanong kung maaaring buksan ang kahong nasa inyo. Wala akong tutol dito; tiyak na ipinadala ko ang kahon sa museo, at kung ipinadala ko ito kay Doktor Jagor at hindi sa inyo, ito ay dahil si Doktor Jagor ang unang nagsabi sa akin tungkol dito. Ipinagpapaumanhin ko iyon.
quote.de: Doktor Wilhelm Joest hat mir geschrieben und gefragt, ob die Kiste, die Sie dort haben, geöffnet werden darf. Ich habe nichts dagegen; gewiss habe ich die Kiste an das Museum gesandt, und wenn ich sie an Doktor Jagor und nicht an Sie schickte, so nur, weil Doktor Jagor mir zuerst davon erzählt hat. Ich bitte dafür um Entschuldigung.

quoteSource.en: Rizal to Adolf Bastian, London, 3 July 1888
quoteSource.fil: Rizal kay Adolf Bastian, London, 3 Hulyo 1888

bio.en:
Wilhelm Joest, an ethnographer, geographer, author, and collector, made his way back home to Europe in 1882 after spending three years in Asia to learn about its cultures. That same year, Rizal traveled the reverse of Joest's route to start his medical studies in Barcelona, Spain.

Apart from being cosmopolitan travelers, Rizal and Joest's family backgrounds were quite similar. Both came from landed families and had opportunities to travel to a different continent using support earned from their family's business. Joest was a son of a sugar manufacturer which allowed him to travel to Northern Africa, Canada and the Americas in 1874 and in 1876 until 1878. Rizal, meanwhile, was able to go to Europe for studies.

During Joest's trips, he collected souvenirs which later became part of his collection. He met Adolf Bastian of the Museum für Völkerkunde around 1879 and became a disciple. Joest shared Bastian's vision of collecting original objects from colonized territories before they get washed out by the colonial culture. From then on, Joest became a collector of Asian and African objects. He had approximately 5,000 collections, many of which were donated to the museums in Europe. Joest's motivation in donating his collections was largely for decorations. His collections included Ainu artefacts, celadon bowls from Seram, and objects from Luzon collected in June 1880. Some of these collections can be found in Cologne's Rautenstrauch-Joest Museum, which was established through the private collections of Joest and his sister Adele.

Joest, a well-known traveler during his prime years, believed that being in situ is more important than theoretical knowledge. He gave lectures about his travels and gained recognition in Berlin's scientific community. His publications include Tattooing, Ornamental Scars and Bodypainting, as well as Um Afrika (About Africa). He finished his doctoral degree in linguistics in 1883 with his thesis on the Gorontalo language. He also helped Rudolf Virchow establish the Museum für deutsche Volkstrachten (Museum for German Traditional Costumes and Domestic Products) in 1889.

In Berlin, Joest and Rizal moved in the same intellectual circles, both acquainted with Adolf Bastian, Rudolf Virchow, and Adolf Bernhard Meyer. Joest also attended several events in scientific society in which Rizal was also present during his stay in the German city in 1886 to 1887. He even wrote an article about Rizal in a Cologne newspaper. Joest was also the one who wrote to Rizal to inquire and confirm his donation of the 21 ethnographic objects to the Museum für Völkerkunde.
bio.fil:
Si Wilhelm Joest, isang etnograpo, heograpo, may-akda, at kolektor, ay nagbalik sa Europa noong 1882 matapos ang tatlong taon sa Asya upang pag-aralan ang mga kultura nito. Sa taon ding iyon, tinahak ni Rizal ang kasalungat ng ruta ni Joest upang simulan ang kanyang pag-aaral ng medisina sa Barcelona, Espanya.

Bukod sa pagiging mga kosmopolitanong manlalakbay, halos katulad ang pinagmulang pampamilya ni Rizal at ni Joest. Pareho silang mula sa mga pamilyang may lupa at nagkaroon ng pagkakataong maglakbay sa ibang kontinente gamit ang tulong mula sa negosyo ng pamilya. Anak si Joest ng isang gumagawa ng asukal, na naging dahilan upang makapaglakbay siya sa Hilagang Aprika, Canada, at sa Amerika noong 1874 at mula 1876 hanggang 1878. Si Rizal naman ay nakapunta sa Europa upang mag-aral.

Sa mga paglalakbay ni Joest, nangalap siya ng mga alaalang kalaunan ay naging bahagi ng kanyang koleksiyon. Nakilala niya si Adolf Bastian ng Museum für Völkerkunde noong mga 1879 at naging alagad nito. Sinalo ni Joest ang pananaw ni Bastian na mangalap ng orihinal na bagay mula sa mga sinakop na teritoryo bago ito matabunan ng kulturang kolonyal. Mula noon, naging kolektor si Joest ng mga bagay na Asyano at Aprikano. Mayroon siyang mga 5,000 koleksiyon, at marami sa mga ito ang ipinagkaloob sa mga museo sa Europa. Pangunahing pampalamuti ang motibasyon ni Joest sa pagkakaloob ng kanyang koleksiyon. Kabilang sa kanyang koleksiyon ang mga artepaktong Ainu, mangkok na celadon mula Seram, at mga bagay mula Luzon na nakalap noong Hunyo 1880. Matatagpuan ang ilan sa mga koleksiyong ito sa Rautenstrauch-Joest Museum ng Cologne, na itinatag sa pamamagitan ng pribadong koleksiyon ni Joest at ng kanyang kapatid na si Adele.

Si Joest, isang kilalang manlalakbay sa kanyang kasibulan, ay naniniwalang higit na mahalaga ang pagiging in situ kaysa sa kaalamang teoretikal. Nagbigay siya ng panayam hinggil sa kanyang mga paglalakbay at nagkamit ng pagkilala sa siyentipikong sambayanan ng Berlin. Kabilang sa kanyang mga akda ang Tattooing, Ornamental Scars and Bodypainting, gayundin ang Um Afrika (Tungkol sa Aprika). Tinapos niya ang kanyang doktorado sa lingguwistika noong 1883 sa tesis niya hinggil sa wikang Gorontalo. Tumulong din siya kay Rudolf Virchow sa pagtatatag ng Museum für deutsche Volkstrachten noong 1889.

Sa Berlin, gumagalaw si Joest at si Rizal sa parehong bilog na intelektwal, at pareho silang kakilala ni Adolf Bastian, Rudolf Virchow, at Adolf Bernhard Meyer. Dumalo rin si Joest sa ilang pagtitipon ng samahang siyentipiko kung saan naroon din si Rizal sa panahon ng kanyang pananatili sa lungsod na Aleman noong 1886 hanggang 1887. Sumulat pa siya ng artikulo tungkol kay Rizal sa isang pahayagan sa Cologne. Si Joest din ang sumulat kay Rizal upang magtanong at magpatibay sa kanyang pagkakaloob ng 21 bagay na etnograpiko sa Museum für Völkerkunde.
bio.de:
Wilhelm Joest, Ethnograf, Geograf, Autor und Sammler, kehrte 1882 nach drei Jahren in Asien, wo er dessen Kulturen kennenlernte, nach Europa zurück. Im selben Jahr reiste Rizal Joests Route in umgekehrter Richtung, um sein Medizinstudium in Barcelona zu beginnen.

Abgesehen davon, dass beide weltläufige Reisende waren, glichen sich Rizals und Joests familiäre Verhältnisse recht genau. Beide stammten aus begüterten Grundbesitzerfamilien und konnten dank der Einkünfte aus dem Familiengeschäft auf einen anderen Kontinent reisen. Joest war der Sohn eines Zuckerfabrikanten, was ihm 1874 sowie von 1876 bis 1878 Reisen nach Nordafrika, Kanada und in die Amerikas ermöglichte. Rizal wiederum konnte zum Studium nach Europa gehen.

Auf seinen Reisen sammelte Joest Andenken, die später Teil seiner Sammlung wurden. Um 1879 begegnete er Adolf Bastian vom Museum für Völkerkunde und wurde sein Schüler. Joest teilte Bastians Anliegen, originale Objekte aus kolonisierten Gebieten zu sammeln, bevor sie von der Kolonialkultur überformt würden. Von da an sammelte Joest asiatische und afrikanische Objekte. Er besaß etwa 5.000 Stücke, von denen viele an Museen in Europa gingen. Joests Beweggrund beim Verschenken seiner Sammlungen war überwiegend die Ausschmückung. Zu seinen Beständen gehörten Ainu-Artefakte, Seladonschalen aus Seram und Objekte aus Luzon, die er im Juni 1880 erwarb. Einige davon finden sich im Kölner Rautenstrauch-Joest-Museum, das aus den Privatsammlungen Joests und seiner Schwester Adele hervorging.

Joest, zu seinen besten Jahren ein bekannter Reisender, hielt die Anschauung vor Ort für wichtiger als theoretisches Wissen. Er hielt Vorträge über seine Reisen und erwarb sich Anerkennung in der wissenschaftlichen Welt Berlins. Zu seinen Veröffentlichungen zählen Tätowiren, Narbenzeichnen und Körperbemalen sowie Um Afrika. 1883 schloss er seine Promotion in Sprachwissenschaft mit einer Arbeit über die Gorontalo-Sprache ab. Er half zudem Rudolf Virchow 1889 bei der Gründung des Museums für deutsche Volkstrachten und Erzeugnisse des Hausgewerbes.

In Berlin verkehrten Joest und Rizal in denselben geistigen Kreisen; beide waren mit Adolf Bastian, Rudolf Virchow und Adolf Bernhard Meyer bekannt. Joest nahm während Rizals Aufenthalt in der Stadt 1886 bis 1887 auch an mehreren Veranstaltungen der gelehrten Gesellschaft teil, bei denen Rizal ebenfalls anwesend war. Er schrieb sogar einen Artikel über Rizal in einer Kölner Zeitung. Joest war es auch, der Rizal anschrieb, um dessen Schenkung der 21 ethnografischen Objekte an das Museum für Völkerkunde zu erfragen und zu bestätigen.
